course.title: AP World History: Modern
course.description: Understand the people, ideas, and connections that shaped the world from c. 1200 to the present.
course.previewDescription: Explore how states rose, belief systems spread, trade networks connected regions, and revolutions reshaped societies from c. 1200 to the present.

themes.title: Interactions of humans with the environment
themes.question: How did geography, crops, resources, or disease shape choices?
themes.example: Andean terraces made steep slopes more usable for farming.

themes.title: Social interactions and organization
themes.question: Who had status, opportunities, or obligations?
themes.example: Examination preparation favored families that could afford education.

themes.title: Political systems and governance
themes.question: How did rulers gain authority and administer territory?
themes.example: Song officials carried imperial decisions into local government.

themes.title: Economic systems
themes.question: How were goods produced, exchanged, taxed, or distributed?
themes.example: Mali drew revenue from commerce through its territory.

themes.title: Cultural developments and interactions
themes.question: How did beliefs, learning, and artistic practices influence society?
themes.example: Buddhist monasteries connected religious practice with education.

themes.title: Technology and innovation
themes.question: What techniques or tools changed what people could do?
themes.example: Inca roads and knotted records helped officials coordinate resources.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes Maya political organization?
choices: All Maya cities were provinces of the Inca state.
Competing city-states shared cultural traditions without one permanent unified government.
A single elected council governed all Mesoamerica.
Maya political life ended completely before 1200.
questions.explanation: Maya cities had their own rulers and relationships. Political changes did not erase Maya communities or traditions.

questions.prompt: Why was retaining local rulers useful to the Mexica tributary system?
choices: Local leaders could deliver required goods while imperial power enforced obligations.
It prevented the collection of tribute.
It required every subject to move to the capital.
It turned all regional markets into independent empires.
questions.explanation: Indirect administration could reduce the need to replace local institutions while still drawing resources from subject communities.

questions.prompt: What was the main relationship between chinampas and Tenochtitlan’s growth?
choices: Floating rafts moved all crops to the Andes.
The system made regional food production unnecessary.
Chinampas served only as temples without an agricultural function.
Intensive cultivation near the city helped supply a substantial urban population.
questions.explanation: Constructed growing beds and channels increased productive land near the capital. Food supported urban life and specialization.

questions.prompt: How did mit’a obligations strengthen Inca administration?
choices: They selected officials through Confucian examinations.
They replaced every household with a paid military regiment.
They supplied rotating labor for state projects and other needs.
They required European coins for all tax payments.
questions.explanation: The state could mobilize labor for agriculture, infrastructure, and service. This was different from a wage contract or the later colonial mining system.

questions.prompt: What inference is supported by Inca roads, relay messengers, and khipus?
choices: Every Inca resident read alphabetic books.
The state coordinated information and resources across difficult terrain.
Trade required wheeled vehicles across the entire Andes.
Inca communities had no relationship with officials.
questions.explanation: Communication and records supported administration. Complex government did not require an alphabetic script or wheeled transport.

questions.prompt: Which comparison accurately connects farming to geography?
choices: Chinampas used lake environments, while terraces helped manage Andean slopes.
Both techniques depended on identical flat desert conditions.
Terraces were drifting gardens and chinampas were mountain roads.
Neither technique affected usable farmland.
questions.explanation: Both supported cultivation, but each responded to different physical conditions. Similar goals did not require identical technology.

questions.prompt: Why is European disease an unsuitable explanation for Mesa Verde’s thirteenth-century relocation?
choices: No American community ever experienced disease.
All environmental explanations are automatically correct.
Mesa Verde was a Spanish colonial town by 1200.
The relocation preceded European arrival in that region by centuries.
questions.explanation: An explanation must fit the chronology. Environmental and social pressures are relevant; later European contact cannot cause an earlier event.

questions.prompt: What can Cahokia’s large earthen mounds most directly support?
choices: Every resident held the same political rank.
A written constitution identical to China’s governed the city.
The community organized substantial labor and resources.
European architects directed all construction.
questions.explanation: Monuments provide evidence of coordinated work. More evidence is needed to reconstruct specific institutions and social relationships.

choices: A voluntary retail purchase.
An obligation imposed on a subordinate community.
A writing system based on knots.
A Buddhist monastic rule.
questions.explanation: Tribute commonly took the form of goods supplied to a ruling power.

questions.prompt: Which tool helped Inca officials keep records?
choices: Khipus.
Chinampas.
Fiefs.
Civil service examination essays.
questions.explanation: Khipus used knotted cords to record information useful to administration.

questions.prompt: What continued after the decline of many Classic Maya centers?
choices: One permanent empire over all of the Americas.
Government by European monarchs before 1200.
The disappearance of all Maya languages.
Maya communities, traditions, and later political centers.
questions.explanation: Urban decline did not mean the end of Maya peoples.
